lessons.title: Intrinsic Value & Margin of Safety
lessons.description: Understand intrinsic value and Benjamin Graham's margin of safety concept.
learningObjectives: Define intrinsic value and margin of safety
lessons.content:
# Intrinsic Value & Margin of Safety

Value investing is the practice of buying stocks that appear underpriced relative to their intrinsic value — and holding them until the market recognizes their true worth. It was pioneered by Benjamin Graham and perfected by Warren Buffett.

## Core Concept: Intrinsic Value

Intrinsic value is the true economic worth of a company, calculated by estimating future cash flows and discounting them to the present.

## Margin of Safety

> Buy ₹1 of value for ₹0.60. — Benjamin Graham

The margin of safety is the difference between a stock's intrinsic value and its market price.
takeaways: Buy at a discount to intrinsic value to maintain a margin of safety.
lessons.summary: Mastering intrinsic value and margin of safety principles.

quiz.title: Quiz: Intrinsic Value & Margin of Safety

questions.text: What is the margin of safety in value investing?
questions.question: What is the margin of safety in value investing?
options: A stop-loss order placed with a broker
The discount at which a stock is bought below its intrinsic value
The amount of cash held in a portfolio
questions.explanation: Margin of safety is the difference between a calculated intrinsic value and the market purchase price.

questions.text: Who pioneered the concept of Value Investing?
questions.question: Who pioneered the concept of Value Investing?
questions.explanation: Benjamin Graham authored 'The Intelligent Investor' and pioneered value investing principles.

questions.text: According to Benjamin Graham, an investor should ideally pay ₹0.60 for how much intrinsic value?
questions.question: According to Benjamin Graham, an investor should ideally pay ₹0.60 for how much intrinsic value?
questions.explanation: Buying ₹1 of value for ₹0.60 creates a 40% margin of safety buffer.

lessons.title: Economic Moats & Competitive Advantage
lessons.description: Identify durable economic moats that protect company profits over decades.
learningObjectives: Identify brand, switching costs, and network effect moats
lessons.content:
# Economic Moats & Competitive Advantage

An economic moat is a durable competitive advantage that protects a company's long-term profitability.
takeaways: Durable moats protect long-term company profitability.
lessons.summary: Identifying competitive advantages and economic moats.

questions.question: What is an economic moat?
options: A high cash debt tax ratio
A durable competitive advantage that sustains profitability
questions.explanation: An economic moat protects a business from competitors over long periods.

questions.text: Which of the following is an example of a Network Effect moat?
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a Network Effect moat?
options: A small retail shop in a local neighborhood
A platform where more users increase the value for all users (e.g. NSE, Visa)
questions.explanation: Network effects occur when an influx of users makes a platform more valuable for everyone.

questions.text: Why do value investors prefer companies with durable economic moats?
questions.question: Why do value investors prefer companies with durable economic moats?
options: They protect high returns on capital from being eroded by competitors
They guarantee zero stock price volatility
They eliminate all corporate income taxes
questions.explanation: Economic moats defend profits and pricing power against competition over decades.

lessons.title: Financial Metrics for Value Investors
lessons.description: Analyze P/E, P/B, ROE, and Free Cash Flow like Warren Buffett.
learningObjectives: Analyze P/E, P/B, ROE, and Free Cash Flow
lessons.content:
# Financial Metrics for Value Investors

Key ratios used by Warren Buffett to analyze financial statements.
takeaways: Use fundamental financial metrics to evaluate true corporate value.
lessons.summary: Financial ratios for value investing analysis.

questions.text: What does Return on Equity (ROE) measure?
questions.question: What does Return on Equity (ROE) measure?
options: Total company debt divided by assets
How efficiently management generates profit from shareholder equity
The market capitalization of the stock
questions.explanation: ROE = Net Income ÷ Shareholder Equity. Higher ROE indicates efficient capital management.

questions.question: What is the P/E Ratio?
options: Price-to-Earnings Ratio (Share Price ÷ Earnings Per Share)
questions.explanation: P/E compares market share price to company earnings per share.

questions.text: Why do value investors focus on Free Cash Flow (FCF)?
questions.question: Why do value investors focus on Free Cash Flow (FCF)?
options: It represents actual cash generated after operating expenses and CapEx
It is always equal to net accounting profit
It indicates total stock exchange trading volume
questions.explanation: Free Cash Flow measures the real cash available to shareholders after capital expenditures.
